If buoyancy and weight are the only significant vertical forces, a net upward force causes UPWARD ACCELERATION, not necessarily an immediately upward velocity; specify no other vertical forces or drag.

Weight greater than upthrust means downward resultant/acceleration if no other vertical forces; the object may still be moving upward briefly, so 'tends to sink' must not be taught as instant downward motion.

review_theme: Zero resultant does not imply rest
teacher_explanatory_note_or_risk: F_net=15 N up −15 N down = 0 N, assuming the given forces are all vertical forces; this allows rest OR constant velocity.

Water provides upward buoyant force, but an open water-filled mug displaces only the volume excluded by the mug material (and any trapped air), not all the open cavity; support reduction may be modest. Avoid attributing a sealed-vessel displacement.
Initial upward acceleration requires buoyancy greater than weight plus relevant drag/other forces; compressibility may change displaced volume during ascent.
At floating equilibrium the displaced water weighs as much as the entire ship and contents; hull shape does not remove gravity.
For fully submerged rigid fixed-volume object and unchanged g, F_B=ρgV increases with liquid density; not a general claim about freely floating objects.
Ideal F_B=ρgV independent of absolute depth when fluid density, g and rigid object volume remain unchanged; strong density stratification/compressibility can change F_B.
At fixed fluid density and displaced volume F_B is proportional to g; doubling g doubles upthrust.
At fixed fluid density and g, doubled displaced volume doubles F_B; the statement refers to displaced, not total arbitrary object volume.
Equal completely submerged displaced volumes in the same uniform-density water at same g yield equal upthrust regardless of the solids' own weights.
For a static liquid of uniform density P2>P1 at greater h2; bottom pressure pushes upward while upper-face pressure pushes downward.
For a completely immersed right cylinder F_B=ρgAh; doubling h while retaining A changes displaced volume, and thus upthrust, by factor two.
For constant-density static liquid, translating both faces down by equal distance retains separation Δh, so pressure difference ρgΔh stays unchanged.
Hydrostatic pressure gradients produce net buoyancy for immersed objects regardless of whether they float; the full surface force integrates beyond a simple two-face model.

review_theme: Ship loading and maximum safe displacement
teacher_explanatory_note_or_risk: An increased cargo mass requires greater displaced water weight for the new floating equilibrium. This is only possible within hull capacity/freeboard/stability limits; excess cargo can sink a ship.
The hollow hull permits a much larger displacement compared with total ship weight; compact metal still experiences buoyancy, but insufficient for flotation.
